title: Neighbourhoods and module stalks at a singleton finite fibre
statement: Let $\pi:Z\to Y$ be a finite morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], let $z\in Z$, and put $y=\pi(z)$. Suppose $\pi^{-1}(\{y\})=\{z\}$. For every open neighbourhood $U\subseteq Z$ of $z$ there is an open neighbourhood $V\subseteq Y$ of $y$ such that $\pi^{-1}(V)\subseteq U$. For every quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_Z$-module $\mathcal G$ [pqf-def-coherent], the canonical germ map $(\pi_*\mathcal G)_y\to\mathcal G_z$ is an isomorphism of $\mathcal O_{Y,y}$-modules, where the action on $\mathcal G_z$ is through $\pi_z^\sharp:\mathcal O_{Y,y}\to\mathcal O_{Z,z}$. Here $(\pi_*\mathcal G)(W)=\mathcal G(\pi^{-1}W)$ for open $W\subseteq Y$ with scalars restricted along the structure sheaf map [def-pc-module-pullback], and stalks are as in [def-pc-module-stalk-functor].

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-iff-integral-lft], the finite morphism $\pi$ is integral. By [pqf-lem-integral-univclosed], it is universally closed and hence closed. Put $C=Z\setminus U$. This is closed and $y\notin\pi(C)$: a point of $C$ mapping to $y$ would equal $z$, whereas $z\in U$. Thus $V=Y\setminus\pi(C)$ is an open neighbourhood of $y$. If $w\in\pi^{-1}(V)$ were outside $U$, then $\pi(w)\in\pi(C)$, a contradiction. This proves the neighbourhood assertion.

To prove the module assertion, take any affine open neighbourhood $V_0$ of $y$. By [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] and [pqf-def-affine-morphism], $W=\pi^{-1}(V_0)$ is affine and the ring map $A=\mathcal O_Y(V_0)\to B=\mathcal O_Z(W)$ is finite. Use [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-spec-points] on $V_0$ and $W$ to represent $y,z$ by primes $\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q$. A point lies above $y$ precisely when its corresponding prime contracts to $\mathfrak p$: the point prime consists of sections whose germs lie in the maximal ideal, and the stalk maps of a scheme morphism are local. The singleton-fibre hypothesis therefore makes $\mathfrak q$ the unique prime of $B$ above $\mathfrak p$.

Set $M=\mathcal G(W)$. Since $\pi$ is affine, clause (1) of [lem-weil-pbc-affine-pushforward-base-change] says $\pi_*\mathcal G$ is quasi-coherent (take the auxiliary base change to be the identity). Apply [lem-sbc-affine-module-germ-localization] to this module on $V_0$, and to $\mathcal G$ on $W$. Using $(\pi_*\mathcal G)(V_0)=M$, these identify their actual germ maps with localization maps from $M$: at $y$ one inverts $A\setminus\mathfrak p$, and at $z$ one inverts $B\setminus\mathfrak q$. Explicitly the resulting identifications are $(\pi_*\mathcal G)_y\cong M\otimes_A A_{\mathfrak p}$ and $\mathcal G_z\cong M_{\mathfrak q}$. The map $m\otimes(a/s)\mapsto am/s$ and its inverse $m/s\mapsto m\otimes(1/s)$ give the tensor description directly from [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] and [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product].

Apply [lem-trf-unique-prime-localization] with the finite ring map and unique prime of Step 2. Its module comparison is an isomorphism $M\otimes_A A_{\mathfrak p}\to M_{\mathfrak q}$. Through Step 3 it sends $m_y/s_y$ to $m_z/(\pi^\sharp s)_z$ for $m\in M$ and $s\in A\setminus\mathfrak p$. The canonical pushforward-to-source germ map sends $m_y$ to $m_z$ and commutes with multiplication by germs of sections of $A$, so it has exactly this fraction formula. Every element is such a fraction, proving equality with the canonical map. Finally [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization](c) identifies $\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ with $A_{\mathfrak p}$ through $a/s\mapsto a_y/s_y$; the same formula for the ring-sheaf map identifies its action on $\mathcal G_z$ with restriction along $\pi_z^\sharp$. Thus the canonical isomorphism is linear for exactly the action stated in the item.
